Tessa Moreno

gap-008 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I do love him. I hate starting with that every time I say I want to go somewhere. Reading with kids is fun when it is something I picked. At home sometimes it is fun too, and sometimes I count the minutes. I do not know what that says about me. I want to leave for a while and still be somebody my family can call, just maybe not for every little thing.

  • family: Lives with her father, grandmother, and three-year-old half-brother; stepmother works alternating out-of-town weeks.
  • finances: Household expenses are covered, but reliable paid childcare is difficult to arrange locally.
  • geography: Outside Abilene, Texas; long bus ride to school.
  • cultureLanguages: English-speaking home; family traditions center on extended-family meals and local events.
  • school: Small public high school; likes literature discussions and participates inconsistently in clubs.
  • accessOpportunities: Library books, school activities requiring advance transport plans, and substantial everyday contact with a toddler and older adult.
  • Age 4–5

    Tessa liked dancing in the kitchen while her grandmother cooked and collecting tiny shampoo bottles from family trips. Adults sometimes called her a little helper because she handed over spoons. She also threw spectacular tantrums when tired. Family videos remind her that being helpful was only one part of her childhood.

  • Age 6–7

    At six she liked reading the same picture book to younger cousins and making funny voices. She became cross when they skipped pages. Her father taught her to ride a bicycle in a parking lot, and she spent an entire summer trying to beat her own circuit time rather than racing anyone else.

  • Age 8–9

    At eight her grandmother had knee surgery. Tessa brought books and cups of water when asked, while adults handled treatment and mobility advice. She liked the long conversations during recovery. She also avoided the room some afternoons because the television was always on and she wanted the adults to watch her new tricks.

  • Age 10–11

    At ten she joined a library reading activity and discovered that some younger children wanted to talk instead of listen. She enjoyed inventing questions more than enforcing quiet. A librarian helped her end sessions at the scheduled time. Otherwise she kept staying because she worried leaving would look unfriendly.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve her half-brother was born and she loved making him laugh. As he grew, short visits became regular responsibilities during changing work arrangements. Tessa could settle him with familiar songs, but she was not always glad to be available. A friend complained that every invitation required a family discussion.

  • Age 14–15

    At fourteen she helped run a supervised story hour and enjoyed it more than unplanned childcare at home. The clear start, finish, and available adults mattered. Online friends praised her for being mature, which felt good until she noticed she was hiding ordinary anger to keep that description. She stopped posting family updates so often.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen she still enjoys reading to children and talking with her grandmother. She has negotiated one protected afternoon each week, though emergencies sometimes swallow it. She wants to attend a residential program after high school and feels disloyal saying so. She is good at familiar care routines and unsure whether she wants more of them.

Life now

  • enjoys: Reading aloud · Grandmother’s stories · Making her brother laugh
  • avoids: Unplanned extra childcare · Being called mature as a reason to give her more work
  • activities: Occasional supervised story hour · Regular sibling care · Literature discussion group when transport works
  • demonstratedSkills: Adapts familiar stories for younger listeners · Recognizes her brother’s routines · Maintains patient conversation with her grandmother
  • unfamiliarActivities: Care for unfamiliar adults · Living away from home · Sustained independent coursework outside school
  • motivations: Close relationships · Time that belongs to her
  • ambitions: Attend a residential learning program after high school · Protect a weekly afternoon for friends
  • struggles: Guilt when setting limits · Missed invitations · Anger she finds hard to admit
  • supports: Librarian who enforces session boundaries · Grandmother who listens · Father increasingly willing to plan care
  • practicalConstraints: Long school bus journey · Limited local childcare · Changing adult work schedules

Still uncertain: How would chosen, bounded care feel compared with family obligation? · Can her plan to study away become practically possible?

Six scores & initial pathways

R, I, A, S, E, C: 20 / 20 / 28 / 24 / 20 / 20, each out of 40. Interests, not ability or success odds.

Pathways: Design & creativity

Work-led options: Teaching & learning · Food, hospitality & personal care

Field explored: education. Tessa chooses bounded storytelling and learning activities because she enjoys adapting stories at supervised story hour more than unlimited home childcare. Wanting time away and liking children can coexist; the choice is an exploration of chosen sessions, not an obligation to continue family care as work.
